original_question: How should the notions of general fractional integrals and general fractional derivatives, originally developed on the positive real semi-axis using Sonine-type kernels and convolution formulas, be adapted to functions defined on a finite interval and on the whole real line R?
target_in_paper: Section 2.4, open problem 8: “Adjust the notions of the GFIs and GFDs to the case of a finite interval and R,” interpreted in the precise framework of Section 2.3, where GFIs/GFDs are defined on the positive real semi-axis R_+=(0,∞) via Sonine-kernel convolution formulas and, in the arbitrary-order setting, via kernel pairs (κ,k)∈L_n.
correct_elements: Your draft already identifies the right open problem very closely: it is about the paper’s general fractional integrals and general fractional derivatives (GFIs/GFDs), it correctly places their existing development on the positive real semi-axis, it mentions the Sonine-kernel/convolution origin of the construction, and it correctly asks for the extension to both a finite interval and the whole line R.
missing_details: The exact target is open problem 8 in Section 2.4, not the earlier open problems about one-parameter fractional integrals/derivatives on finite intervals.
The existing theory being extended is the Section 2.3 GFI/GFD framework on R_+=(0,∞), where the operators are one-sided convolution operators with lower limit 0.
In the arbitrary-order formulation, one fixes n∈N and a kernel pair (κ,k)∈L_n satisfying κ∈C_{-1}(0,+∞), k∈C_{-1,0}(0,+∞), and the generalized Sonine relation (κ∗k)(t)=h_n(t)=t^{n−1}/(n−1)! for t>0.
The paper distinguishes two derivative notions that should be adapted: the Riemann–Liouville-type GFD and the Caputo-type GFD.

The Caputo-type arbitrary-order definition uses subtraction of the initial polynomial term Σ_{j=0}^{n−1} f^(j)(0) h_{j+1}; a stand-alone question should make clear that the role of this distinguished endpoint data must also be reconsidered on [a,b] and on R.

The nearby context justifies the names GFI/GFD through analogues of the first and second fundamental theorems of fractional calculus (Theorems 8 and 9), so the adaptation is not merely a change of domain notation.
The natural function spaces in the current theory include C_{-1}(0,+∞), C_{-1,(k)}(0,+∞), C_{-1,(κ)}(0,+∞), and C^n_{-1}(0,+∞); your draft does not mention these admissible spaces.

The paper does not impose any ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, or nilpotency conditions here; the missing technical content is instead the kernel class, the domain, the operator formulas, the endpoint terms, and the function-space hypotheses.
refined_question: In the Section 2.3 framework of general fractional calculus, for a fixed n∈N and a kernel pair (κ,k)∈L_n with κ∈C_{-1}(0,+∞), k∈C_{-1,0}(0,+∞), and (κ∗k)(t)=h_n(t)=t^{n−1}/(n−1)! on R_+=(0,∞), the general fractional integral and the associated Riemann–Liouville- and Caputo-type general fractional derivatives are defined by one-sided convolution formulas on t>0, namely (I_(κ)f)(t)=∫_0^t κ(t−τ)f(τ)dτ, (D_(k)f)(t)=d^n/dt^n ∫_0^t k(t−τ)f(τ)dτ, and (∗D_(k)f)(t)=D_(k)(f−Σ_{j=0}^{n−1}f^(j)(0)h_{j+1})(t). How should these notions be reformulated for functions defined on a finite interval [a,b] and on the whole real line R, with appropriate kernel classes, convolution structure, endpoint/initial-data terms, and function spaces, so that they extend the paper’s GFI/GFD framework and admit analogues of the fundamental-theorem identities proved on R_+?
justification: The draft matches open problem 8 almost verbatim. Section 2.3 introduces the paper’s GFIs/GFDs only for functions on the positive real semi-axis, first through Sonine-kernel convolution formulas and then, more generally, for arbitrary order via the classes L_n and formulas (47)–(49). Theorems 8 and 9 explain what makes these operators the relevant “notions” of GFI/GFD in the paper. Section 2.4 then asks exactly to move those notions to a finite interval and to R. This is therefore narrower and more faithful than the neighboring open problem 4, which concerns the earlier one-parameter fractional-integral/fractional-derivative problems rather than the GFI/GFD framework itself.
